Presidential RamblingsBy Steve Hansen
Our last demo prior to the summer break could
have been sub-titled “like watching paint dry” as
Larry Stevenson gave an informative talk about the
various paint products that he uses on his beautiful
work. Of course the talk was anything but boring.
During the summer the Guild held a club picnic
that was fairly well attended and an auction coincided which put about 45 items into the hands of
our members and selling on average at about 1/3
retail. We netted about $1000. The vast amount of
items were donated by Bob Gadd of Woodworkers
Specialties – thank you Bob! Other donors were Ed
Pretty, Dan Breck, Ross Patterson. The Guild itself
liquidated a few superfluous items, and the Cindy
Drozda demo piece from 2020 went to a lucky bidder.
Our meeting schedule and format going into the
new season will continue exactly as before.
For those asking about upcoming classes, the Guild
needs to remedy the slippery floor of the KMS
workshop. The problem all started a few years ago
when we held a soap stone turning event the ensuing dust that covered all shop surfaces is very slippery and our initial attempts to make the floor nonskid have failed. Please stay tuned.
October’s challenge is “Small Treasures” – something that fits inside 16 cubic inches.
Steve

This Month’s CoverBy Theo Vriezen
This simple walnut centerpiece was the removed
pith out of the crotch area of the tree. It was completely sealed with a wood end seal and left to dry.
I had fully expected to later find a twisted, checked
or split piece of nothing. It however remained stable and was milled down to a 13" x 14" x 1" slab.
The soft area was cleaned out and filled with black
resin. A 4.5" dished area was turned with the use
of a donut chuck and a finish of walnut oil and wax
was applied.
This piece has managed to hold on to a coveted
spot on the dining room table, regularly adorned
with various potted plants, translucent polished
stones and probably a gourd before the month is
out.

Turning Lemons into LemonadeBy Cathy Friesen
Over a year ago I began a project to make a lamp
for my soon-to-be niece. I started by turning a
lamp out of three pieces of birch. The grain was
very pretty and I thought I could make it look even
nicer for a child's room by changing its colour.
Using an Aniline Wood Stain I started by dying the
lamp a dark blue.
As I didn't know whether the baby was going to be
a girl or a boy at the time I decided that a more
gender neutral color would be turquoise. So I dyed
the blue lamp again with a yellow dye. But unfortunately the color that appeared was a really ugly
green. I was quite disappointed in the lamp but I
thought with some high gloss wipe-on poly it
would look pretty anyway so I finished the lamp to
completion.
But every time I looked at it I felt it was not good
enough to give to somebody I cared about, so
Grace arrived and I had no gift to give her. I left the
lamp out on my counter for months trying to figure
out what I was going to do with it. One day I just
got fed up, took it back out to the lathe and sanded
off as much of the color as I could.
The results actually looked quite nice. The green
mixed with the grain of the wood gave a kind of
underwater feel to the lamp. So I decided to capitalize on that.

KMS Tools Group Rewards
Shopping at KMS Tools means you can help your
club earn credit - approximately 2% on your purchase. For instance, we recently used some of our
credit to buy the brand-new Laguna demo lathe
that we use for Focus on Fundamentals! All you
need to do is to link your name/phone number to
the GVWG and you’re done. The easiest way to do
this is to go online to: https://www.kmstools.com/
group-rewards and fill in a short form. In doing so,
you also become a KMS Club member and benefit
from better pricing on their full line of products. As
a friendly reminder if you are already a KMS Club
member, it is worthwhile to check that you are also
linked to the GVWG for us to receive the credits.

Are You Turning Too Fast?By Larry Stevenson
My decision to write this article came after viewing
a video tape from our library. For those of you
whom would like to review for yourself it is V41 –
2001 AAW Symposium, Techniques Video, Volume
One. In particular this article was a result of a discussion by Dale Nish on Natural Edge Bowls. He
was discussing that many turners are turning, in his
opinion, at too fast a speed. He goes on to mention that he has been called as a witness at trials
involving deaths resulting from injuries related to
“turning too fast”. He mentioned a particular case
where a friend of his was turning large 24” Lazy
Susans and received an extremely bad injury from
turning too fast and may have been better off if he
hadn’t survived. His injury left him dependent on
having medical devices attached to him indefinitely. The long and the short of it is that Dale Nish
recommends that you use the following formula to
determine a safe turning speed.
DIAMETER * RPM = 6000 – 9000
The numbers 6000 – 9000 are just numbers that
are used to determine a range of safe turning
speeds. I thought I’d do a little math and found out
that I have definitely been guilty of exceeding this
limit. So here is a table of speeds using the preceding formula.
Now I know that most of the lathes out there either do not have a digital RPM readout or do not
have all this range of speeds, however this does
provide a guideline for “Safe Turning Speeds”.
Next time I have a large platter on the lathe I will
probably exercise on the side of caution as I really
enjoy woodturning and would hate to have a delamination or breakage send me to the hospital.
Obviously, this doesn’t negate the need for proper
eye and face protection, it is just meant as another
guideline for safety.

Firstly I suggest that you view this demo on
YouTube by Michael DeMeng on using Kroma
Crackle and he has coined the phrase “Demented
Derma”. It is well worth watching and it contributed to my playing with this product.
https://youtu.be/KfR3V3JWd5I
I am interested in textures and playing with different methods has always been interesting to me.
When Joanne Sauvageau joined our guild I went to
her website and was viewing her images and this
one struck me as extremely interesting. It is a
beautiful piece and I thought that I needed to play
with the medium used to create this even more.
During the president’s challenge during our online
Covid meetings one of the challenges was to do a
spalted piece. I had several entries into that challenge based on some smaller rounds that I had cut
out of some spalted maple and this piece used the
method of shrinking up some Kroma Crackle on
various coloured base colours and dry brushing
some metallic colours on them.
I then wanted to increase the size of this on a larger bowl and this was the result. I made a horrible
mistake and didn’t tint the crackle first. I was planning on over-coating later but the crackle was quite
thin and trying to over-coat it was painful and
couldn’t be done without getting paint in the
cracks, so I had to bite the bullet and hand paint
each and every flake which ended up being easier
to do with a tooth pick. It took me about 27 hours
to paint the blue on this piece but I figured that
was the lesson this dumb ass had to learn.
(Continued on page 8)
Kroma Crackle Demo
- June 2023
By Larry Stevenson
Joanne Sauvageau piece from her website
Piece I have done since
Big mistake made on this bowl, I didn’t add colour
to crackle and had to paint each speck by hand

September 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
I have done other bowls and as you will see during
this demo “Kroma Crackle” is a fairly thin gel with
the consistency of a hair gel product and it doesn’t
dry fast. Putting it on a three dimensional surface
is a trick because it wants to run all over the place.
Kroma says let it start to set in the container mixed
with the paint first and then try but it is still a pain
to work with on large three dimensional objects.
With this bowl I but the bowl on a jamb chuck and
put it on the lathe turning extremely slowly and
used the heat gun to start the setting process.
Here is the issue that you need to be aware of. I
have a Oneway 2436 lathe and turning at such slow
speeds the motor overheats. When this happens,
the controller detects it and shuts the motor off.
Then the product sags and starts moving where
you don’t want it. All motors are cooled by a built
in fan which works fine when the motor is turning
at some respectable RPM but not down in the single digit of RPM. How could we avoid this overheating? We could find a different way of driving
the object being held in the lathe such as rigging up
a rotisserie motor to drive the object or maybe using a fan directly on the motor to cool it down. I
haven’t tried either of these yet so if you try them
and they work, let me know.
This next bowl was done again with pre-colouring
the crackle and putting it on again with a spatula
but not doing it on the lathe. I did this one upside
down on a stand and did a little bit at a time and
partially dried it as I went with the heat gun. All of
these pieces have been over sprayed with water
based lacquer or urethane finish to protect the
crackle from falling off or being picked off by people whom just can’t control themselves or want to
buy this piece even after they have destroyed part
of it. BE WARNED. Please keep your picking fingers in your pockets or better yet go home and do
this yourself and pick away to you hearts content,
only do it to your own pieces.
Another president’s challenge was a teapot. There
is a picture that I will share in Mary Fox’s book on
“My Life as a Potter” that was partially responsible
for this piece. I love her work and do own one of
her pieces. Anyway, later picture to show her
piece. I didn’t have lots of time to do a new piece
so I took a dried form destined to be an urn for a
pet and used the body to make this piece. The
handle brought up the question on how to position
the grain as to make the handle not susceptible to
breaking or cracking. I decided to use a piece of
maple burl, not a fancy one but burl none the less.
That way the grain comes from many directions all
twisted up and very strong. The spout is just a
plain piece of maple made into a spout shape and
glued on with epoxy as was the handle. The lid is
nothing special although I borrowed the form from
the urns I turn. This is about the finish after all.
Wood is sealed and the base coat is a bright red
(Continued from page 7)
(Continued on page 9)
The pooling of crackle on this bowl is due to lathe
shutting off due to overheating and crackle
sagged.
This bowl was made for my sister-in-law

September 2023

Page 9
color over a white undercoat. I did this as the red I
was using was a transparent paint and the white
underneath showed the colour better. Then the
Kroma Crackle was tinted with a black acrylic paint
and applied in small batches and partially dried
with the heat gun before I moved on to the next
application. I dry brushed on some grey on the tips
of some of the crackle flakes to imitate ash. The
entire piece was then over-coated with water
based lacquer.
Here is an image of the container for Kroma Crackle. It is available directly from Kroma on Granville
Island. It does come in various sizes. It is also
available from Opus as well as other art stores I’m
sure.
Here is a small test board. It has two coats of Golden Titanium White as a basecoat thinned with a bit
of airbrush medium. It then had a coat of Kroma
Crackle applied. The Kroma Crackle can be mixed
up to 10% by weight of acrylic paints. Don’t rely on
my numbers look at the literature. I was allowed
to dry unaided and took about two days. Some of
the flakes become prominent and can easily be
picked off. If you do this you will have your knuckle
rapped very hard. DON’T DO IT. The way the
patterns form at the edges are totally natural and
in brick layers terms this is called soldiering.
Here is a picture of the Golden product called Golden Crackle Paste. It is much lighter, almost like a
whipped up cream of some sort.
(Continued from page 8)
(Continued on page 10)
“Hot Tea” a president’s challenge piece. Constructed of a dry urn form with added handle,
spout and lid.
Kroma Crackle – allowed to dry slowly (about 2
days)
Golden Crackle Paste

On this test board. It has two coats of Golden Titanium White as a basecoat thinned with a bit of airbrush medium. It then had a similar coating of this
Golden Crackle medium mixed with cobalt blue
acrylic. It again dried in about 2 days and here is
the result. Not as splendid a result as the Kroma
product in my mind but maybe this is the finish or
texture you would want if you were doing a
painting. Just not what I wanted doing my projects.
This next test board has the undercoats like the
last ones only there has been a coat of white glue
(Titebond Type 1) applied and dried first. I then
applied equal thicknesses of Kroma on the left and
Golden on the right. They both have the same
amount of Golden Cobalt Blue added and mixed in
and then they were dried with the heat gun. The
Kroma product shrunk up and I deliberately shrunk
the centre up to show you how much you can do
with this product. That mountain in the centre basically is most of the medium from the sample. On
the right the Golden product just dried up and no
cracks appeared at all.
Other sample boards. Here are some older sample
boards. This first on is on a blue background and
shows it over-coated with an acrylic lacquer or urethane. These products stabilize the individual
flakes of finish. Again a good example of the natural soldiering on the edges.
This sample board has had sand blasting medium
added to the finish. The one on the left the
crushed glass as added on top of the medium and
the right the crushed glass was added into the medium before it was applied.
(Continued from page 9)

(about 2 days)
Heat Shrunk with Gun (both crackles)
Other Sample Board

Here is a sample board with a black background
with the Kroma Crackle dried up with a heat gun
and then various metallic paints dry brushed over
it. You can mix up a wash or do whatever methods
come to your mind. You just play.
This sample board was a bit of a mistake but the
results were intriguing. It had the white background and then I applied the Brite Red via airbrush. I don’t believe I applied the glue next.
When the crackle was applied and dried with the
heat gun it pulled the red away with it partially exposing the white. Interesting and possibly something to experiment with.
Sources of Inspiration
Earlier I mentioned Mary Fox. She is a potter that
resides in Ladysmith and I would advise anyone to
pay her a visit. She makes stunning works and has
won several awards. This piece was a gift from my
brother and sister in law for taking care of my
mother’s estate and given to me after they purchased one of the bowls shown earlier. It reminded them of Mary’s pottery and as a result I have
this wonderful piece. I just love the textures that
she creates in her pottery. A very gifted artist indeed.
They also got me a book about Mary Fox and there
are many great images that I cannot share in this
presentation due to copyrights but this is one of
the benefits for actually coming to the hall as you
can browse this book and look at her terrific works.
OK, this slide is a blank that has been prepared to
add colour to. It has had two coats of Golden Titanium White applied first then various colours applied without much discretion or thought. They are
merely there to give a varied background. Remember we are here to play, I am not making any works
(Continued from page 10)
(Continued on page 12)
Sources of Inspiration
Book about Mary Fox

September 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 12
of art that are destined to be in a gallery somewhere. We will dry brush various colour on the
surface to create interest. On top of the coloured
background I have applied Kroma Crackle and dried
it with the heat gun. There are thin layers and
thick layers, how it is applied and dried is up to
your discretion. There is one rule that is kind of
obvious once you have started playing with this
stuff and that is “The thicker the application the
bigger the flakes or scales” whatever you want to
call them.
(Continued from page 11)
One of the reasons I bought a lathe was to turn
components for models. Primarily I am making
scale airplanes from solid wood, mostly in 1:48
scale. Wheels are the most common part, but small
shafts are needed as well.
For a small diversion, I am making a bottled
schooner model which has two masts. Masts on
boats are generally long tapers from base to top.
Models of this scale, approximately 1:450, means
the masts are at the most 1/16” diameter at the
base and about half that at the top over a length of
about 2”.
Typically the dowel is held into a drill and moved
back and forth between sandpaper, whether hand
held or on a bench. But hey, I have a lathe which
makes things a bit more controlled.
I double taped an 6”x3/4” 80 grit paper to a piece
of 3/4x 1” scrap that also works as a sanding block
for shaping parts.
Using a 3/4x1/4x 6” scrap, cut a shallow “V”
groove across it about 1” from the end. This groove
keeps the dowel from simply trying to run down
the length of the blocks when it is being sanded.
A collet set has become my go to tools for turning
small stuff. Using the 1/16” collet, mount the work
in about 1” leaving a 3” section of mast free hanging (allows a bit of room for waste).
Holding the “V” groove block under the part, lay
the dowel in the groove. Place the sanding block
over top the work and lightly hold the two blocks
(Continued on page 13)
Creating Long Tapers for Modelling and MiniaturesBy Fraser MacLean

September 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 13
together with the part in the groove.
Turn on the lathe to about 1700 rpm and lightly
squeeze the blocks together and move item towards the lathe head stock. Move at a constant
speed from the end and as you are moving the
blocks along, gradually reduce the pressure to zero
at the butt end. As you repeat this, it will form a
gradual taper of the piece.
The taper can be varied by the distance traveled
and the pressure on the blocks. If you apply the
sanding only to the end you can get a short taper.
Working center to either end will cut a concave. By
changing the profile of the sanding block: cove,
round, narrow etc, various profiles could be made
at vary small diameters over a relatively long
length.
For final sanding, overlay a piece of finer grit paper
directly over the 80 grit on the block. The 80 grit
will keep the second paper from sliding off.
(Continued from page 12)
Alone Together By Sheila Balzer
-GVWG WIT Liaison
Documenting the beginner’s journey has certainly
been an interesting process and sharing it with others continues to be a practice of summarizing and
capturing these experiences.
These summer months have been super busy with
a wide array of activities, and sadly I discovered
that there are goldilocks conditions for me to get
into my shop…not too hot…not too cold, but just
right. This summer, at least in the beginning, was
way too hot. Despite the conditions and constraints, my woodturning journey did continue and
even flourished.
Woodturning is inherently a task that one does on
their own, in their own company, and going
through their own process of finding the chunk of
material to transform into something else. This
(Continued on page 14)
Sheila and Donna

September 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 14
reality struck me even more so during a delightful
visit to see Donna in Tlell on Haida Gwaii. Amongst
the trees and berry bushes, next to the sea, there
she is with her shop, tools, and woodshed, taking
chunks of wood and making them into something
else. It was curious to see how she learns and
turns, practices, and plays and achieves some
sweet results. There are failures/mistakes too, but
Donna has an effective way of thinking through the
challenges at hand and working her way though to
the final presentation. There really are not many
people who have ever seen her turn. And until we
captured some video of her at the lathe, she had
never seen herself turn. But alone in her shop, her
sanctuary, she gets out as often as she can and
plays at her process, mostly all alone and figures it
out. It truly was a privilege to be welcomed into
her sanctuary to take a turn to turn too. (Added to
my wish list…One Way 16/40…and a bigger shop…
but not by much).
It was a fun experience during our visit together
that we raided her friend’s firewood pile for chunks
of yellow cedar, that got transformed into a workable blank, and turned into an egg-shaped rattle. I
would have been inclined to just use the rough
shaped hunk of wood, but her efforts made it safer
and more balanced to begin the project. We both
tapped into the lessons and tips that Art Liestman
had shared during one of his presentations about
form, which included the formation of an egg. It
was shocking of how many eggs got made before
we consistently marked the blank, egg, plug to
make the grain match an easier process. Glue
joints are something we both want to explore and
practice more. The first ones took a while. We debated the merit of shaping the outside first before
hollowing vs doing the shaping afterwards. Shaping before worked better as doing it afterwards led
to a failure because “one more cut” made it too
thin to sand through all the grits. Slowly, each egg
got made a little faster. And although we each did
the turning alone, it was fun and enjoyable process
to turn them together.
I am so thankful that when Donna and I met during
one of the online WIT Exchanges, she took up the
invitation to join the GVWG as a member. I look
forward to continuing to encourage, cheer, and
cajole her to play, practice, and share her lessons
learned. I doubt she fully realizes just how much
wisdom and knowledge she has that others would
love to learn too.
Which segways into another journey embraced this
summer. Did you know that GVWG formalized a
(Continued from page 13)
(Continued on page 15)

September 2023
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 15
process for certification of its members to do
demonstrations in public on behalf of the GVWG?
This summer I did that process and became certified. You can too.
I jumped these hoops so I could do my first public
demonstration at the Arts Alive event in Langley,
BC held August 19th, along with Dan Moleschi, and
coordinated by Lin & Jay Mapson. It was a thrill to
be at the lathe, sharing my love of turning, with a
wide variety of people including those who turn,
those who know nothing about it, kids…I especially
like the kids, and some who just might be curious
about checking it out for themselves…in their spare
time.
Some of the reasons why I personally am in favour
of the certification process is to have a simple process to check in and ensure that when in public and
showing others how much we enjoy being at the
lathe and making stuff, that there are some basics
we all will consistently practice and do, especially
in the name of safety. While I, as a new turner
made discoveries during the process, such as the
need to begin with a balanced chunk of wood, free
from challenges such as knots and cracks, many of
the more established turners will need to simply go
through that check list and agree to practice these
standards while turning in public too. Given the
wide array of visual materials on turning that exist
today, I can appreciate the requirement of this process to have each of our members, turning in public spaces, to have the same consistent practices.
Why go through this process? Why do public
demonstrations? Why share your gift of
knowledge with others?
For me, it has been one of the ways I get to challenge myself and become a better turner. The conversations, the interactions, the sharing of what is
possible was a complete joy. How many seeds got
planted? How many others just might discover this
world of woodturning because of a chance encounter? Who knew that I just might become a production turner with my first sale ever because of a
chance encounter from this event? However, I
recognize, while this brings energy and growth for
me and my style of learning, for others, this would
bring on anxiety and terror…or would it?
Being a member of the guild, being part of a worldwide woodturning community, even though I may
turn alone, my life has been forever enriched by
the opportunities and connections I’ve made. And
I’m only at the beginning of this journey. Others
have known and experienced this connection far
longer, but I’m so glad that so many of the people
in this community have been willing to share their
experiences to help bring me and others further
along their own discoveries. And I look forward to
the continued efforts of many to share what they
have learned and practiced along their way. Although we might do our turning alone, it’s the experiences of turning together that keeps me coming
back for more.

Understanding Moisture Content Is Important for WoodturnersBy Eric Wagner, Wagner Moisture Meters, Rogue River, Oregon, USA
Successful woodturning, just like all woodworking,
requires careful management of wood moisture
content. Moisture content is an important factor
in how wood works, plus in the durability and
lasting beauty of the finished product.
Understanding Moisture Content
All wood contains moisture. Wood is a hygroscopic
material, which means it easily absorbs or releases
moisture. The moisture in the surrounding air determines the moisture content (MC) of wood. Relative humidity (RH) measures moisture in the air.
It represents how much water the air holds compared to how much it could hold at a given temperature and pressure.
As RH increases, wood absorbs moisture from the
air, which causes it to expand. As RH decreases,
wood releases moisture into the air, which causes
it to shrink. MC is the ratio of the weight of water
in a piece of wood compared to the weight of the
wood without water. The formula is:
MC = (weight of water / weight of dry wood) x 100
For example, a 10 lb. block of wood (as measured
once it’s dry), containing 1 lb. of water has an MC
of: (1 / (10 – 1)) x 100 = 11.1 %
The Importance of Controlling MC
Wood expands and contracts as its MC changes.
So, if MC is allowed to drop significantly after a
piece has been turned, the wood can shrink, crack
or warp. Warping occurs because wood shrinks
more in the direction of the grain than it does
across the grain, or because the wood is unevenly
dried. This means MC must be kept steady within
about ±2% through the process of making wood
products and all the way through when the product is in service.
RH and Equilibrium Moisture Content
As we saw, MC is determined by the relative humidity of the surrounding air. As RH increases,
wood absorbs moisture. As RH decreases, wood
releases moisture to the air. When the RH is in balance with MC, the exchange of moisture stops.
This is called the equilibrium point, and the MC of
the wood at this point is called the equilibrium
moisture content (EMC).
To avoid problems with expansion and contraction,
keep the wood at an EMC close to the value where
the product will be used. For most indoor spaces
in North America, the average RH is 30% to 50%,
which corresponds to an EMC of 6% to 9%.
Moisture Problems in Wood Turning
Improper MC can cause problems when you’re

turning the wood. If the MC is too high, the wood
fibers will be weak, and the wood will not turn
smoothly. If MC is too low, the wood can crack or
chip.
Uneven drying can also cause problems. Wood
that was dried too quickly can have a higher MC in
the center than on the surface. This causes the
surface to shrink more than the centre and creates
stress inside the wood. When the wood is turned,
the stress is released, and the wood warps.
Wood can also dry unevenly because moisture is
released from the end-grain faster than it is along
the grain.
Because wood shrinks across the grain more than it
does along the grain, too much shrinkage after the
wood is turned can cause the piece to warp.
How Twice Turning Can Help Control Shrinkage
Twice turning reduces blank drying time, ensures
smooth turning, and prevents cracks and warping
after the piece is turned.
As the name implies, it is a two-step process. First,
a green blank is turned to remove most of the
waste material. Then the piece is allowed additional time to dry. With most of the waste material
removed, the piece will dry much faster than the
whole blank would.
As the wood dries, the piece will naturally distort.
Once the wood reaches the correct MC, the final
turning removes the remaining waste material and
produces the final shape. With the correct MC, the
piece will not shrink or distort after the final turning.
Controlling Moisture Content
Moisture control begins long before you start turning. There are several sources of wood for turning,
and MC can vary widely depending on which type
you choose.
Many woodturners like to start with green wood.
Green wood is freshly sawn and has not been
dried. The nice thing about green wood is that you
can choose a piece with more character than a
piece of kiln-dried lumber, and it can be inexpensive or free.
Kiln drying uses heat and air circulation to speed up
the drying process. Kiln-dried wood is dried to an
MC of about 8%, which makes it ready for turning.
The drawback is that it’s relatively expensive. Airdried wood is less expensive than kiln-dried, but
it’s usually only dried to about 10% to 18% MC.
You’ll need to dry this wood further before final
turning.
Drying Wood
If you’re using wood that isn’t dried to the proper
6% to 9% MC, you’ll need to dry it yourself. There
are several ways to do this. First, you can air-dry it
by keeping it in an enclosed space that’s conditioned 30% to 50% RH. Drying this way can take
many months, but it’s inexpensive and it ensures
slow, even drying. You can also kiln-dry it by using
a home-made kiln. If you have a small, enclosed
space, you can provide heat with regular incandescent light bulbs. Some people have had success
with drying wood with a microwave oven; however, there can be problems if this is not done cor-
(Continued from page 16)
(Continued on page 18)

rectly or done too fast. The end grain dries faster
than the rest of the wood. You can ensure more
even drying by protecting the end grain with a coat
of a product like Anchorseal.
Using a Scale to Determine When Wood Is
Dry:
As wood dries and approaches its EMC, drying
slows and eventually stops. You can tell when this
happens by weighing the wood. You need to do
this in your controlled space that you keep at 30%
to 50% RH.
With a precise digital scale, weigh the wood every
few days and record the weight until it stops losing
weight. Once the wood has stabilized, it is at the
correct MC and is ready to be turned.
Using a Scale to Precisely Measure MC
You can also measure the exact MC by using a
scale. This is a more complicated and tedious process, and it requires a very precise scale. It also
requires an oven for drying the wood. Wood releases toxic chemicals as it is drying, so the oven
must be dedicated strictly to this purpose.
First, cut a small block about 1” on the side from
the wood you want to measure. Weigh the block to
within a tenth of an ounce and record it. This is
called the “initial weight.”
Next, dry the block in an oven at about 210 to 220
degrees Fahrenheit. You’ll need to dry it for about
24 hours. Then weigh the wood every few hours
and record the weight. When the wood stops losing weight, it is dry.
Weigh the block and record the weight. This is the
“oven-dry weight.” Then use the two weights to
calculate MC using this formula:
MC = ((initial weight – oven dry weight) x 100 ) /
oven-dry weight
Measuring MC with a Moisture Meter
Measuring MC with a scale is time-consuming and
tedious. Moisture meters can make it faster and
more convenient. There are two types of moisture
meters available: pin-type meters and pinless meters.
Pin-type meters use the electrical resistance of
moisture in the wood to measure the wood’s MC.
The meter has two metal pins that you push into
the wood to the desired depth. The resistance is
measured between the pins. The lower the resistance, the higher the MC.
Pin-type meters are sensitive to temperature, so
they usually come with a temperature correction
chart. They’re also sensitive to the chemical
makeup of the wood species, so a species setting is
usually provided.
The orientation of the wood grain also affects the
reading, so you need to drive the pins at the correct orientation.
Pinless meters send an electromagnetic signal
through the wood that measures the wood’s dielectric properties. To take a reading, you place the
meter on a flat surface of the wood. The reading is
available in seconds. There are no pins to mar the
surface of the wood. There is no time wasted hammering the pins into the wood, so a pinless meter
can be much faster to use.
Pinless meters are sensitive to wood density and
come with a species setting to compensate. To
measure at different depths, use a good pinless
(Continued from page 17)
(Continued on page 19)

meter that has a selectable depth setting. Grain
orientation does not affect the readings in pinless
meters.
Wood moisture meters are much faster and easier,
and are more reliable than using a scale to measure MC.
Pinless meters have these advantages over pintype meters:
•
They don’t mar the wood surface,
•
They don’t require orienting and driving pins,
•
There are no pins to bend or break,
•
They are unaffected by temperature and grain
orientation, and
•
They are faster and easier to use.

Safety Guidelines for WoodturningYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock
(Continued on page 29)

with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
